evidence_set: Among men who currently used snus and no other tobacco, against never-users of tobacco, by years of snus use at baseline, all-cause aHR rose from 1.08 (0.88–1.32) under 5 years to 1.29 (1.20–1.38) at 15 years or more (p for trend 0.001); cardiovascular and other-cause deaths showed the same pattern (p for trend 0.001 each), cancer did not (0.11). Few deaths sit in the shorter categories (13 cardiovascular deaths under 5 years). By weekly amount, all-cause aHR was 1.28 (under 4 cans), 1.17 (4 to 6) and 1.37 (7 or more), p for trend 0.09; the cardiovascular ratio was highest in the lightest group (1.44, 1.18, 1.17; p for trend 0.03), the other-cause ratio highest in the heaviest (1.24, 1.18, 1.65; p for trend 0.001), and cancer showed no pattern (p for trend 0.22). The abstract says risks did not increase with weekly amount; the trends by amount differ by cause.

Leaving out the Construction Worker Cohort raised the all-cause, cardiovascular and cancer ratios for current snus use against never use of tobacco: all-cause 1.42 (1.21–1.66), cardiovascular 1.39 (1.05–1.84), cancer 1.52 (1.15–1.99); the other-cause ratio was 1.34 (0.97–1.86), against 1.37 in the full analysis, and its interval now includes 1. That cohort supplied 87% of the deaths in the current snus group (1,233 of 1,410) and 66% of those in the never-used group (6,116 of 9,272) (editors' arithmetic from Tables 3 and 4). Follow-up capped at 10 years: all-cause 1.34 (1.21–1.48), cancer 1.24 (1.02–1.52), other causes 1.57 (1.35–1.83), but cardiovascular 1.13 (0.93–1.38), no longer distinguishable from no difference; the authors say the cardiovascular result should be read with caution because of this inconsistency. Extra adjustment for education, alcohol and physical activity in six cohorts (158 snus-group deaths): all-cause 1.46 (1.22–1.75), cardiovascular 1.56 (1.14–2.14), cancer 1.51 (1.12–2.03), other causes 1.20 (0.83–1.72).

The current snus group was younger (mean age 29 against 38 years), drank more (37.9% in the highest alcohol tertile against 20.2%) and more often had 10 to 12 years of education (52.6% against 38.7%) than men who never used tobacco (the alcohol and education percentages are within the cohorts that recorded them, which leaves out the Construction Workers Cohort); body mass index was similar (24.1 against 24.6). The authors name residual confounding and a single baseline measurement of exposure as weaknesses, and describe their findings as supporting an association, with public-health relevance if it is causal. Their suggested explanations (nicotine effects on blood vessels and heart rhythm, tumour promotion, poorer cancer survival, alcohol-linked injury and violence, risk-taking) were not tested in these data.

Funding as printed: Department of Public Health Sciences, Karolinska Institutet; Region Vasterbotten; Region Vasternorrland; the Joint Committee of County Councils in Northern Sweden (Visare Norr); the regional agreement between Umea University and Region Vasterbotten (ALF); the Swedish Society of Medicine. The funders are stated to have had no role. Conflicts: none declared. The principal investigator of each contributing cohort supplied the data.
Funding; Conflict of interest; Methods › Contributing studies and data collection, 1st paragraph

Pancreatic cancer in the Construction Workers Cohort, in current snus users at baseline against never users of tobacco, varied with the length of follow-up: HR 1.98 (0.97–4.03, 4 exposed cases) to 1994, 2.1 (1.2–3.6, 18 cases) to 2004, 1.34 (0.90–1.99, 31 cases) to 2013; the pooled nine-cohort analysis (36 years, follow-up to 2013, 41 exposed cases), a sensitivity analysis restricted to never smokers, gave HR 1.07 (0.77–1.50), graded very low. In that pooled analysis two thirds of participants and 72% of cases or deaths came from the Construction Workers Cohort.

Rectal cancer in exclusive current snus users against never users of tobacco: HR 1.38 (1.07–1.77, 73 exposed cases) at 27 years of follow-up in nine pooled cohorts; combining the non-construction cohorts with a 10-years-longer follow-up of the Construction Workers Cohort gave HR 1.10 (0.91–1.34), a drop of about 20% in the point estimate. Colon cancer HR 1.02 to 1.08 and anal cancer 0.61 (0.07–5.07, 1 case) showed no clear difference.

Snus only against no tobacco, estimates close to no difference or lower (except one high but imprecise estimate, noted below): oral cancer (pooled 9 cohorts HR 0.93, 0.59–1.44, 25 exposed cases; a third study of oral and pharyngeal cancers combined, in never-smoking daily users, HR 2.3, 0.7–8.3, 5 cases, whose interval includes no difference), lung cancer RR 0.8 (0.4–1.3, 15 cases), non-Hodgkin lymphoma incidence rate ratio 0.77 (0.59–1.01), Hodgkin lymphoma 0.88 (0.49–1.58; in men who used snus for over 30 years 3.78, 1.23–11.60, 4 cases), leukaemias and myeloma 0.81 to 1.24, all melanoma 0.65 (0.52–0.82); the lymphoma, leukaemia and melanoma results were not graded because they were given as incidence rate ratios.

Mortality: a pooled Swedish analysis of eight cohorts (the Byhamre et al., 2021 study, named as the source of the cancer-specific row in Table 1 and matching it in figures, so counted once) gave, for exclusive current snus users against never users of tobacco, all-cause HR 1.28 (1.20–1.35) and cancer-specific HR 1.12 (1.00–1.26); a separate cohort not in that analysis gave HR 1.23 (1.09–1.40) for all-cause and 1.28 (0.96–1.69) for cancer death in never-smoking men who had ever used snus, against never users of snus. After a cancer diagnosis in construction workers, against patients who never used tobacco, total mortality HR 1.13 (1.05–1.20) and cancer death HR 1.15 (1.05–1.26); after prostate cancer, overall HR 1.19 (1.04–1.37) and prostate cancer death HR 1.24 (1.03–1.49); after colorectal cancer, overall HR 1.16 (0.89–1.50), and 1.89 (1.21–2.94, 22 deaths) when the construction cohort was left out.
Discussion › 4.5 (snus compared with cigarettes), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Figure 4 (values not extracted)

Studies by researchers linked to the tobacco industry or sponsored by it were excluded by design, as were estimates based only on combined snus and cigarette use. Exposure caveats: a single baseline recording of tobacco habits; about 30% of exclusive snus users may later stop or move to smoking (a Swedish study cited); in the paragraph on the Construction Workers Cohort, more than 75% of exclusive snus users were under 30 at entry, against 31% of smokers, and only a small proportion of snus users were traced beyond 70; seven of the included studies used construction-worker data from 1971 to 1975, when non-use could not be told from non-response; 13.2% of never-smoking snus users, against 6.7% of never users of tobacco, had a repeat record showing smoking in one study. All authors declare no conflicts of interest; the page has no funding statement.

The abstract says the additional evidence extends the list of conditions unassociated with snus (oropharynx, oesophagus, stomach, lung) to include colorectal cancer and acoustic neuroma, and further undermines the weakly-based argument that snus raises pancreatic cancer risk. The text reports no new snus study of pancreatic cancer: a pooled analysis of 11 case-control studies of other smokeless tobacco, none in Scandinavia, gave OR 0.98 (0.75–1.27) for ever use, against never users of tobacco; earlier combined Scandinavian cohorts gave 1.61 (0.77–3.34) in people who never smoked. No oesophageal, stomach or lung data are shown in this update, so their listing rests on the 2011 review, which was not read.
Conclusions, 1st paragraph; heart failure: Abstract (last sentences) and Discussion, 4th paragraph

Heart attack or ischaemic heart disease, current against never snus use, in never-smoking Swedish men: 13 estimates pooled, fixed-effect RR 1.07 (0.98–1.16), heterogeneity p = 0.06, random-effects 1.06 (0.91–1.23); leaving out the construction-worker interview estimate of 1971 to 1974 (1.35, 1.13–1.62, fatal cases only) gives 12 estimates, fixed 1.00 (0.91–1.10), random 1.00 (0.88–1.13). Several of the 13 estimates are adjusted for age only.

Case fatality, current against never snus use in male never smokers: in five studies, fatal heart attack RR 1.31 (1.09–1.58) and non-fatal 0.89 (0.79–1.00), ratio 1.48 (1.19–1.84); in the pooled eight-cohort analysis (men who never smoked) incidence RR 1.04 (0.93–1.17) and short-term fatality OR 1.28 (0.99–1.68), with the Construction Workers Study 88% of person-years; the author asks whether the fatality excess is a direct effect or confounding. Heart failure: Construction Workers Study RR 1.28 (1.00–1.64) in men who never smoked, with 75 exposed cases, no dose-response by daily amount; Uppsala cohort RR 2.08 (1.03–4.22) with 14 exposed cases, men who smoked and men who did not combined.
